title: Built a free privacy-first tools site, done the on-page SEO, now totally stuck on getting listed anywhere. Which directories still actually matter in 2026?
summary: Hey everyone, hoping for some honest advice from people who do this properly. I built a site called Practical Tools. It's a big collection of free online tools, over 170 of them (calculators, converters, image and video tools, that kind of thing). The thing that actually makes it different is that the file tools all run in your browser. Nothing gets uploaded, no account, no sign up. So if you remove a photo background or compress a video, the file never leaves your device. I care a lot about that privacy angle and it's genuinely how the whole thing is built. I've spent a long time on the on-page side. Sitemap, structured data, real content on each tool page, an llms.txt, fast pages, mobile friendly. I think that part is in reasonable shape now. Where I'm completely stuck is off-page. I have basically no backlinks and the site isn't listed anywhere yet. I know directories are part of the answer, but the space feels like a minefield. Half of them look like link farms and I really don't want to hurt my domain by getting listed in junk. So my questions for the people who've actually done this: Which directories are genuinely worth it in 2026? Free or paid, I just want ones that still carry weight and won't hurt me. Are there any that are good specifically for free tools or indie web apps? How do you tell a legit directory from a link farm before you submit? Beyond directories, what actually moved the needle for you on early backlinks when you were starting from nothing? I'm not looking for anyone to link me out of pity. I'd genuinely just appreciate pointers from people who've built this part up before, because I feel like I'm missing something obvious. Happy to drop the link in the comments if it helps for context. I didn't want to lead with it and come across as spammy. Thanks a lot for reading.   submitted by   /u/digital_mopad [link]   [comments]

title: How would you structure a modern first-pass SEO audit in 2026?
summary: Hey everyone, I’m trying to improve how I approach first-pass SEO audits and would appreciate input from people who regularly work on technical SEO, agency SEO, freelance audits, or in-house site reviews. I’m not talking about a full deep audit with competitor research, log file analysis, stakeholder interviews, content strategy, backlink review, and business context. I mean the first layer of checks you would normally review when looking at a new website before deciding where to dig deeper. For a quick first-pass audit, I’m thinking the core areas should include technical SEO, on-page SEO, meta titles and descriptions, heading structure, indexability, crawlability, robots.txt, XML sitemap, canonical tags, internal linking, broken links, duplicate content signals, keyword cannibalization signals, schema and structured data, HTML validation, Core Web Vitals, page speed, mobile usability, image SEO, link analysis, and general content quality signals. I’m also thinking about whether AI-search-related checks should now be part of the first-pass audit process. More SEO conversations seem to be moving beyond traditional Google rankings, especially with clients asking about answer engines, AI-generated responses, and visibility in generative search experiences. Because of that, I’m considering whether checks like AI crawler access, structured data readiness, entity clarity, AEO signals, and GEO signals should be reviewed early or kept as a separate layer after the traditional SEO audit. My main question is: for a modern first-pass SEO audit, what would you consider essential, and what would you consider nice-to-have? I’m especially interested in how other SEOs separate technical SEO, content, performance, structured data, and AI-search readiness when reviewing a site for the first time. I’m also curious how you would score or prioritize these areas. Would you keep everything under one general SEO score, or would you separate it into categories such as technical health, content quality, crawlability, performance, structured data, and AI-search readiness? I want to avoid focusing on vanity checks that look good in a report but do not actually help decision-making or improve organic performance. For those who run audits regularly, which checks usually reveal the most useful insights early on? Which checks do you think are often overvalued? Would you include AEO and GEO in a first-pass audit in 2026, or would you keep them separate from traditional SEO? I’d appreciate any thoughts from people who have a practical audit process and know what actually helps move from diagnosis to action.   submitted by   /u/Apprehensive-Job3344 [link]   [comments]
